newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: India seeking more control over diesel imports.
newsitem.headline: India seeking more control over diesel imports.

text.p: State-owned Indian Oil Corp (IOC) is seeking more diesel through long-term purchase contracts so that it can tighten control over import flows and payments, trading sources said on Tuesday.
Term contracts would allow IOC to plan longer term, especially at its ports which have been plagued by congestion for many years.
The IOC is in the midst of annual negotiations to set up term buying contracts and has already raised some import volumes.
Traders said IOC is negotiating with Saudi Aramco to buy about one million tonnes of diesel during January-December 1997. IOC did not buy any diesel on a term basis from Aramco in 1996.
India already has long-standing annual term deals with three other Middle East national oil companies.
Last month, IOC raised diesel imports from the Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) for fiscal 1996-1997 (April-March) to 1.68 million tonnes from 1.5 million tonnes covered by the year-earlier contract.
On Monday, the IOC renewed a contract with Abu Dhabi National Oil Co (ADNOC), maintaining diesel at 500,000 tonnes.
It will start talks with Bahrain National Oil Co (BANOCO) next week. Under the 1995-1996 deal, IOC bought 1.32 million tonnes of diesel from BANOCO.
But sources said the IOC probably also took part in Saudi Aramco's annual term tender to sell diesel and other products, which closed on Monday, or was negotiating directly with the Gulf oil giant.
Sources said term deals would allow IOC to better control import payments and be less exposed to price volatility. It could also tighten its hold over the quality of imports.
It could manage the discharge of cargoes better and ease congestion, the sources said.

Tankers normally have to wait three to four weeks before discharging diesel owing to congestion. By mid September there were 1.173 million tonnes of diesel deliveries waiting to discharge at India's ports.

The congestion problems have prompted IOC to cut monthly spot tender purchases of its staple 0.5-percent sulphur diesel to none in November from 120,000 tonnes in October and as much as 1.5 million tonnes in June.

Speaking at the IOC annual meeting on Monday, Chairman R.K. Narang said "there is a time lag and a bit of queuing up," at the ports, but stressed the IOC would focus on infrastructure projects in coming years to ease the congestion.
Trade sources estimated that demurrage claims against IOC owing to delays were $10 million to $15 million a month.

They said IOC is considering putting a cap on what shipowners can receive and standardise demurrage rates to cut demurrage costs. On the other hand, IOC might then have to pay higher premiums for its imports to compensate for the cap on demurrage claims.
Diesel demand in India is growing 14.5 percent a year. The IOC has projected diesel demand will grow from 35 million tonnes in 1996/1997 to 54 million tonnes by 2001/2002.
